props.title: 8MM

sections.content: **8mm** (1999) plunges into the grimy underbelly of underground filmmaking through Nicolas Cage's private investigator Tom Welles. Like **Se7en** (1995) before it, the film weaponizes audience discomfort by keeping the most disturbing content just off-screen. Director Joel Schumacher, fresh off the critically panned **Batman & Robin** (1997), returned to darker territory reminiscent of his earlier **Falling Down** (1993). The film shares DNA with other late 90s neo-noir investigations like **Lost Highway** (1997) and **Dark City** (1998), examining how far someone will go to expose hidden truths.

sections.content: The film's examination of snuff films and exploitation connects directly to Michael Powell's **Peeping Tom** (1960), which destroyed his career by forcing audiences to confront voyeuristic violence. **8mm** carries this thread through to the digital age, alongside films like **Strange Days** (1995) and **Tesis** (1996) that wrestle with recorded violence. Joaquin Phoenix's adult bookstore clerk Max California serves as Welles' Virgil, guiding him through increasingly disturbing circles of underground film. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Investigative Horror

While **8mm** focuses on analog horror, its DNA lives on in found footage films like **Sinister** (2012) and digital-age investigations like **Searching** (2018). The film's lasting influence shows in works like **Nightcrawler** (2014), where Jake Gyllenhaal's character represents the evolution of media exploitation into mainstream news. Even Nicolas Winding Refn's series **Too Old to Die Young** (2019) echoes similar themes of investigators becoming corrupted by what they uncover.
